title: "Motion and Shifts as Weapons"
subtitle: "Why NFL offenses now move someone before most snaps, what each kind of motion is for, and how to read the defense's answer before the ball is snapped."
description: "The motion family (jet, fly, rocket, orbit, return, zoom, glide, trade, short motion and the shift to bunch) and motion at the snap; the five jobs motion does (reading man or zone, changing strength and numbers, leverage, a running start, stressing communication); the defense's answers (travel, bump, spin) and why the man/zone indicator sometimes lies; the NFL, college and CFL motion rules and the 2024 'cheat motion' language; the 2016-2025 motion boom in PFF, FTN, ESPN and Next Gen Stats numbers and why they disagree; and the watching checklist after Part 2."
glossary:
  "Jet motion": "A receiver (or back) sprinting across the formation, parallel to the line, timed so that the ball is snapped just before he reaches the quarterback. He is at full speed at the snap, ready to take a jet sweep or to fake one."
  "Fly motion": "The Wing-T's name for jet-style motion: a wingback or slot sprinting across the formation behind an under-center quarterback, usually for the fly sweep. Many teams use 'fly' and 'jet' for the same thing."
  "Orbit motion": "Motion that loops behind the quarterback: a receiver comes in toward the ball, swings around behind the quarterback (and the back), and is still moving toward the far side at the snap."
  "Rocket motion": {def: "A fast motion by a back, deep in the backfield and straight out toward the sideline, so he is already running wide at the snap. The classic play is the rocket toss, a pitch to him at the edge.", aliases: ["Rock motion"]}
  "Return motion": {def: "Motion that goes one way and then reverses back toward where it started, usually at or just before the snap. It makes a defender who followed the first move stop and restart, and lets the offense watch the defense react twice.", aliases: ["Yo-yo motion", "Yo-yo"]}
  "Zoom motion": "Motion all the way across the formation that ends with the player set on the other side (in some playbooks it is the Z receiver's motion, hence the Z in the name), changing the formation, typically from 2x2 into 3x1."
  "Glide motion": "A wide receiver motioning from a wide spot in toward the ball, with the snap coming when he is about halfway there, so he starts the play already moving inside: good for crossing routes and crack blocks."
  "Trade (TE trade)": "The tight end changing sides of the formation before the snap, usually as part of a shift in which a receiver also steps on or off the line. It flips the formation's strength, so the defense has to re-declare."
  "Short motion": {def: "A motion of only a few yards, usually a receiver tightening his split or tucking in beside or behind a teammate, often set again before the snap. Some offensive playbooks call it rip (right) and liz (left), the same words many defenses use for their strength call.", aliases: ["Rip/liz motion"]}
  "Motion at the snap": "Motion timed so that the player is still moving when the ball is snapped. It describes timing, not a path: jet, orbit, glide, rocket and return motion are usually run this way. NFL rules allow it for one backfield player moving parallel to or away from the line."
  "Man/zone indicator": "Reading the defense's reaction to motion as a clue to its coverage: a defender who follows the motion man across suggests man coverage; defenders who shuffle over without following suggest zone. A strong hint, not a guarantee."
  "Travel (man defender follows motion)": "A defender running with a player in motion and staying with him across the formation. The classic sign of man coverage."
  "Bump (defensive adjustment)": "Defenders sliding one spot toward the motion instead of following it, so nobody crosses the formation. It is the usual zone answer, but man defenses slide too (an exchange), so a bump alone does not prove zone: look at where the slid defenders end up."
  "Exchange (man coverage on motion)": "A man-coverage answer to motion in which nobody follows the motion man across: the defenders slide over and swap receivers, so the defender on the side he arrives at picks him up. From the stands it looks like a zone bump; the difference is that each slid defender ends up squared up close on one receiver."
  "Spin (safety rotation on motion)": "The safeties rotating in answer to motion: one comes down (usually on the side the motion is heading to, sometimes the other side) and the other moves to the deep middle, so two deep safeties become one."

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import logging
import os
import shutil
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from IPython.display import HTML, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, routes as r, style
from gridiron.animate import animate
from gridiron.play import MARKER_R

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- building plays by hand
def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(d=-0.7):
    """The five offensive linemen (only the center labelled)."""
    return [O(k, k, d, w, label="C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


def gun_2x1_te(z_w=15.0):
    """11 personnel from the gun: X on the line to the left, H in the left slot, the tight end (Y)
    attached on the right and Z a step off the ball outside him. Seven on the line (five linemen, X
    and Y), so Z, H, the back and the quarterback are backfield players: any one of them may go in motion."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, z_w, "Z")]


def gun_2x2_spread():
    """11 personnel 2x2 with the tight end flexed into the right slot; X and Z on the line."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -1.5, 9.0, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z")]


def under_wing():
    """Under center: tight end on the right, a wingback (H) just outside and behind him, a tailback."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                     O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                     O("H", "WR", -1.6, 6.4, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 15.0, "Z")]


def front4(sde=4.3):
    """A four-man front against a tight end on the right (the end on that side outside the tackle)."""
    return [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "T"),
            D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "T"), D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, sde, "E")]


def dashed_motion(p, key, to, head=0.5):
    """Pre-snap movement to the spot `to` (absolute d, w), drawn dashed with a short solid head.
    (gridiron draws the last part of a path's final segment solid, so one long segment would
    look like a route.)"""
    d0, w0 = p._cur(key)
    dd, dw = to[0] - d0, to[1] - w0
    f = max(0.0, 1 - head / float(np.hypot(dd, dw)))
    p.motion(key, pts=[(dd * f, dw * f), (dd, dw)])


def schedule(p, plan):
    """Re-time pre-snap movement. plan = {key: (t_start, t_end)} in seconds from the snap.
    gridiron ends every pre-snap motion exactly at the snap and starts it whenever its length and
    speed require, so two players who should move together drift apart. This stretches each listed
    player's pre-snap path into his window (and holds him still until the snap if it ends early).
    Implemented here rather than in gridiron; call it after every action has been added."""
    kf, t0, t1 = p._compile()
    for key, (a, b) in plan.items():
        arr = kf[key]
        pre, post = arr[arr[:, 0] <= 1e-9], arr[arr[:, 0] > 1e-9]
        T0, T1 = pre[0, 0], pre[-1, 0]
        new = pre.copy()
        new[:, 0] = a + (pre[:, 0] - T0) / ((T1 - T0) or 1.0) * (b - a)
        rows = [new] + ([np.array([[0.0, *new[-1, 1:]]])] if b < 0 else []) + [post]
        kf[key] = np.vstack(rows)
    p._compiled = (kf, min(float(f[0, 0]) for f in kf.values()), t1)
    return p


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing helpers
def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard numbers (in these zoomed windows they sit where players stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def P_of(fld, p):
    """(d, w) in the play's frame -> plot coordinates on this field."""
    return lambda d, w: tuple(float(v) for v in fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w)))


def tag(ax, xy, text, ec=style.BASELINE, fs=6.8, lw=0.6, ha="center"):
    ax.text(*xy, text, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, linespacing=1.15,
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=lw))


def callout(ax, P, text, at, to, fs=6.8, ec=style.BASELINE):
    """A label at `at` with a thin leader line to `to` (both (d, w))."""
    ax.annotate(text, xy=P(*to), xytext=P(*at), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12,
                linespacing=1.15, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=0.6),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=4))


def ghost_marker(ax, x, y, label, ppy, side="def"):
    """A hollow, dashed marker: where a player stood before he moved."""
    col = style.DEFENSE if side == "def" else style.OFFENSE
    if side == "def":
        pat = RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARKER_R * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4, facecolor="none",
                             edgecolor=col, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6)
    else:
        pat = Circle((x, y), MARKER_R, facecolor="none", edgecolor=col, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6)
    ax.add_patch(pat)
    if label:
        ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", color=col, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
                fontsize=max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * 0.72)))


def mpath(ax, P, pts, kind="pre"):
    """A path through (d, w) points drawn by hand. 'pre' = pre-snap motion (dashed, blue);
    'post' = what he does after the snap (thin, solid, grey)."""
    col = style.OFFENSE if kind == "pre" else style.INK_2
    xy = [P(d, w) for d, w in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    lw = 1.6 if kind == "pre" else 1.0
    cut = (xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2]))
    ax.plot(list(xs[:-1]) + [cut[0]], list(ys[:-1]) + [cut[1]], color=col, lw=lw,
            ls=(0, (3, 2)) if kind == "pre" else "-", zorder=5, solid_capstyle="round")
    head = (xs[-2] + 0.7 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.7 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2]))
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(head, xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=8, color=col, lw=lw,
                                 shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, zorder=5))


def dpath(ax, P, a, b):
    """A defender's pre-snap slide, dashed, in the defense's colour."""
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(P(*a), P(*b), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=7, color=style.DEFENSE,
                                 lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=5, shrinkB=5, zorder=4))


def snap_dot(ax, P, at, dd=-1.4, dw=0.0):
    """Mark where the moving player is when the ball is snapped."""
    x, y = P(*at)
    ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.6, color=style.BALL, zorder=9)
    ax.text(*P(at[0] + dd, at[1] + dw), "snap", fontsize=6.2, color=style.BALL, ha="center", va="center",
            zorder=9, style="italic")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- animations and their print strips
def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 15.5), ghosts=(), ghost_t=None, notes=()):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, a faint trail behind each mover since the first frame, and a
    hollow 'ghost' where each listed player stood at `ghost_t`."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for n in notes:
        q.note(*n)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    no_numbers(ax)
    P = P_of(fld, play)
    start = play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT", "NT"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(start, t, 40)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.4:
            continue
        xs, ys = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]))
        col = style.OFFENSE if pl.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=col, lw=1.2, alpha=0.55, ls="-" if pl.side == "off" else (0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    if ghost_t is not None:
        for k in ghosts:
            d0, w0 = play.position(k, ghost_t)
            d1, w1 = play.position(k, t)
            if abs(d1 - d0) + abs(w1 - w0) > 1.0:
                ghost_marker(ax, *P(d0, w0), play.players[k].label, ppy, play.players[k].side)
    bd, bw = play.ball_position(t)
    carried = any(np.hypot(*(play.position(k, t) - np.array([bd, bw]))) < 0.3
                  for k, pl in play.players.items() if pl.side == "off" and k != "C")
    bx, by = P(bd + (0.95 if carried and t > 0 else 0.0), bw)   # a carried ball sits just in front of him
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 0.75, 1.1, facecolor=style.BALL, edgecolor="white", lw=0.6, zorder=9.5))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, ncols=2, **kw):
    """The print version of an animation: one panel per chosen moment, each with a caption."""
    lateral, window = kw.get("lateral", (-21, 21)), kw.get("window", (-8.5, 15.5))
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = 6.5 / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.36) + 0.35
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(6.5, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for ax, t, lab in zip(axes.flat, times, labels):
        snapshot(play, t, ax=ax, **kw)
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left", pad=3)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.5, rect=(0, 0.05, 1, 1))
    hs = [Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, alpha=0.7, label="Offense: path so far"),
          Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defense: path so far"),
          Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), label="Dashed outline: where he started")]
    fig.legend(handles=hs, loc="lower center", ncol=3, fontsize=7.2, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0))
    return fig


def show_play(play, times, labels, web_caption, **kw):
    """Web: an animation with a caption that changes with the phase of the play.
    Print: a labelled frame strip (panel titles = `labels`)."""
    if PDF:
        strip(play, times, labels, **kw)
        plt.show()
        return
    df = play.to_tracking()
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    anim = animate(df, to_go=play.to_go)
    ax = anim._fig.axes[0]
    cap = ax.text(0.01, 0.02, "", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=style.INK,
                  zorder=21, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.THIRD, lw=1.0))
    base = anim._func

    def upd(fid, *a):
        out = base(fid, *a)
        cap.set_text(web_caption(float(tmap.get(fid, 0.0))))
        return out
    anim._func = upd
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(anim._fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def phases(cuts):
    """[(t_upper, caption), ...] -> function of t (seconds from the snap) for show_play."""
    def f(t):
        for up, txt in cuts:
            if t < up:
                return txt
        return cuts[-1][1]
    return f
```

First-and-10, early in the second quarter. The receiver split wide on the right turns and jogs
toward the ball, then breaks into a sprint, running flat along the line, across the whole
formation. The cornerback who had been standing seven yards in front of him turns and runs too,
step for step, all the way across the field. "There's your man coverage," says the analyst, and
before he finishes the sentence the ball is snapped, the receiver takes a little flip from the
quarterback without breaking stride, and he is ten yards upfield before the corner chasing him
can turn the corner. How did the analyst know? Why did the offense want him to know? And if the
run was coming anyway, why didn't the defense simply let the receiver go? This chapter is about
the most common thing an NFL offense does before the snap, moving somebody, and about what each
kind of movement is for.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name the common motions on sight: **jet**, **fly**, **rocket**, **orbit**, **return
  (yo-yo)**, **zoom**, **glide**, **short (rip/liz)**, the tight end **trade** and the **shift to
  bunch**, and say when a motion is happening **at the snap**.
- Explain the five jobs motion does: it asks *man or zone?*, changes the formation's strength and
  numbers, gives a player a running start, creates leverage, and stresses the defense's
  communication.
- Read the defense's answer as it happens (a defender **travels**, the defense **bumps**, or the
  safeties **spin**) and turn it into a coverage guess, tell a zone bump from a man **exchange**,
  and know when the guess can be wrong.
- Explain how the NFL's motion rule differs from college and Canadian football, and what the
  2024 rule language written after the "cheat motion" did and didn't change.
- Describe the 2016–2025 motion boom with numbers, and explain why PFF, FTN, ESPN and Next Gen
  Stats publish such different motion rates.
- Run the **watching checklist so far**: situation → personnel → formation and strength → the
  motion response → box → shell.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **The pre-snap rules** ([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)):
  after a [shift](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shift) (two or more players moving at once)
  everyone must be [set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-set) for a full second; in
  [motion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion) only one backfield player may be moving at the
  snap, parallel to or away from the line, never toward it.
- **Formations** ([Spread and Modern Formations](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)):
  [2x2](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) is two receivers on each side,
  [3x1 (trips)](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) three to one side and one to the other, a
  [bunch](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) is three receivers squeezed into a tight
  triangle, and an [empty](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) set has no back beside the
  quarterback. The side with more players (usually the tight end's side) is the
  [strength](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd).
- **A first look at defense** ([A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  in [man coverage](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) each defender is assigned a receiver; in
  [zone coverage](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) each is assigned an area. The safeties'
  picture is [one-high](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) (one deep in the middle) or
  [two-high](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) (two deep, one per side), and the
  [box](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) is the area near the ball where run defenders stand.
  Counting blockers against box defenders tells you whether the run has the numbers.

## Motion has a job

[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) gave you the rules (who may
move, which way, and when everyone has to freeze) and three reasons motion exists: it asks the
defense a question, it gives a player a running start, and it changes the formation late. The
rules set the shape: a receiver running across the formation moves *flat*, parallel to the line,
because he may not be angling toward it at the snap, and two receivers never sprint at the snap
together, because only one player may be moving. This chapter splits those three reasons into
five jobs, gives every kind of motion a name, and shows you how to read the defense's answer.

Here is the idea to hold on to: **no good offense moves a player for decoration.** Kyle
Shanahan, whose 49ers have been among the league's heaviest motion users since 2017, put it
plainly: "You do it for a reason. You do it to help one of your players or you do it because you
see something that you think will affect the defense." Sean McVay of the Rams added the warning
every coach repeats: "It's not just to look cool."[^espn2022]

Every motion does one or more of five jobs:

1. **It asks a question: man or zone?** Someone on the defense has to deal with the moving
   player, and *how* they deal with him is a clue to the coverage.
2. **It changes the strength and the numbers.** A player who moves from one side to the other
   changes how many receivers (or blockers) are on each side, and the defense has to rebalance in
   a second or two.
3. **It gives a running start.** A player moving at the snap is already at speed when the play
   begins, and nobody on the defense is.
4. **It creates leverage.** A defender's position relative to his receiver, inside or outside,
   in front or behind, is planned against a *standing* receiver. A moving one changes it.
5. **It stresses communication.** Each time the formation changes, the defense has to
   re-declare its calls, and every re-declared call is a chance for two defenders to take the
   same man and none to take another.

The costs from [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) still apply
(play-clock time, precise timing, and the risk of tipping the play), and this chapter adds one
more when it reaches motion at the snap. First, the vocabulary: the motions themselves.

## The motion family

Motions are named by **path** (where the player goes) and **timing** (whether he is still moving
when the ball is snapped). Here is the family the rest of this book uses.

``` {.python .cell-code}
LAT_F, WIN_F = (-18.5, 18.5), (-8.6, 2.6)
PANELS = []


def panel(fn):
    PANELS.append(fn)
    return fn


def base(ax, off, ring=()):
    p = Play(off, None, los=50, to_go=None)
    p.highlight(*ring)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_F, window=WIN_F)
    return fld, P_of(fld, p)


@panel
def f_jet(ax):
    fld, P = base(ax, gun_2x1_te(), ("Z",))
    mpath(ax, P, [(-1.5, 15), (-2.6, 9), (-3.0, 4), (-3.1, 1.2)])
    mpath(ax, P, [(-3.1, 1.2), (-3.2, -3.6), (-1.4, -6.4)], kind="post")
    snap_dot(ax, P, (-3.1, 1.2), dd=-0.9, dw=3.6)
    return "Jet", "full speed across, in front of the gun QB"


@panel
def f_fly(ax):
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Jet motion" sounds like a technical term with one meaning. It isn't. Motion names are
**playbook dialect**: each staff names its motions in its own language, often after the letter of
the player who moves ("zip" and "zoom" for the Z receiver, "yo-yo" for Y), and the same word can
mean different things in two buildings. Some teams use *jet* and *fly* for the same motion; some
use *orbit* only for a running back. The names below are the common ones in NFL film breakdowns
and coaching clinics, and the glossary records them.[^names] Learn the **shapes**, and you'll
recognise the motion whatever the broadcast calls it.
:::

**Motions that cross the formation.** These are the big, fast ones, almost always timed so the
ball is snapped while the player is still moving.

- [**Jet motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jet-motion): a receiver sprints across the
  formation, flat along the line, timed so that the ball is snapped just *before* he reaches the
  quarterback. In the shotgun he passes between the quarterback and the line, close enough to take
  a handoff or a little forward flip (the [jet sweep](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd),
  a run to the edge by the motion man himself). That little flip travels forward, so in the rules
  it is a forward pass: if it hits the ground it is an incomplete pass, not a fumble.[^popflip] Most of the time he doesn't get the ball at all: the jet is a
  *threat*, and the defense has to respect it either way.
- [**Fly motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fly-motion): the older name for the same idea
  from the [Wing-T](02-03-classic-formations.qmd), a run-heavy offense of the 1950s onward. A wingback (a back lined up just
  outside and behind the tight end) sprints across behind an under-center quarterback, who turns
  and hands him the ball on the "fly sweep." Many staffs say *jet* and *fly* interchangeably.
  Where they distinguish them, *fly* is usually the under-center version, with the runner passing
  behind the quarterback.
- [**Orbit motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-orbit-motion): a receiver comes in toward
  the ball and swings *behind* the quarterback (and behind the back), like a moon around a
  planet, and is still moving toward the far side at the snap. Going behind the quarterback means
  he can take a pitch or a shovel pass (a short underhand toss), or turn into a receiver out of
  the backfield, and he is
  harder for the defense to track because he disappears behind the offensive line for a moment.
- [**Zoom motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zoom-motion): a receiver goes all the way
  across the formation and then *sets* on the other side, usually as the new inside receiver
  (#3, counting from the sideline in). It isn't about speed; it is about the new formation. A 2x2
  becomes a 3x1, and the defense has to rebalance (Job 2, below).

**Motions out of the backfield.**

- [**Rocket motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rocket-motion) (also **rock motion**): a
  back sprints from his spot in the backfield straight out toward the sideline, staying deep,
  so he is already running wide when the ball is snapped. In option offenses such as the [flexbone](02-03-classic-formations.qmd)
  the same name is used for a slotback (a back set just behind the line, outside the tackle)
  sprinting on a deep path behind the quarterback.[^rocket] The play it sets up is the **rocket
  toss**, a pitch to the back at the edge, and the rocket motion is a fine way to get a back into
  a pass route with a head start, too.

**Motions that come back, or come in.** These are subtler, and they matter most in the passing
game.

- [**Return motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-return-motion) (also **yo-yo motion** or
  **yo-yo**): a receiver motions one way, then reverses back toward where he started, usually
  right at the snap. Its targets are the defenders who follow motion: whoever chased the first
  move is now running the wrong way.
- [**Glide motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-glide-motion): a wide receiver motions in
  toward the ball at a controlled pace, and the snap comes when he is about halfway to the
  formation, and he is *still moving* when the ball is snapped (that is the difference from short
  motion, which stops and sets). He starts the play already moving inside, which helps a crossing
  route, a quick break back outside, or a [crack block](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) (a receiver blocking back inside on a linebacker or safety,
  taught with the perimeter runs in [Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd)).
- [**Short motion**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-short-motion) (also **rip/liz motion**,
  after the "right" and "left" tags some playbooks use): a few yards and no more, usually a receiver
  tightening his split, or tucking in beside or behind a teammate to form a
  [stack](02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd), and usually set again before the snap. Short
  motion looks like nothing, which is part of the point: a receiver who starts closer to the ball
  has more room to the outside, and a defender who lined up against his old spot is a step out of
  place. (Don't confuse these rip/liz tags with the Rip/Liz *strength call* from
  [Formation Rules](02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd): the same two words are a direction
  tag in some offensive playbooks and the defense's strength call in others.)

**Moves that change the whole formation.** These are usually *shifts*, because more than one
player moves.

- A [**trade**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trade-te-trade) (a **TE trade**): the tight end
  changes sides. Because he leaves the line, someone else has to keep the offense legal (seven on
  the line, with only the end men eligible): usually a receiver on the new side steps *off* the
  line and one on the old side steps *on*, all at once. The strength flips, and the defense has to
  flip its front and its coverage calls with it. Because a trade is a shift, the offense must then
  hold still for a full second, which guarantees the defense that beat to re-set; offenses often
  follow the trade with a motion to take it back. (You saw a trade, and the defense flipping in
  answer, in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).)
- The **shift to bunch**: three receivers squeeze into a tight triangle at the last moment. Against
  man coverage a bunch is a traffic jam that defenders have to fight through (the crossing routes
  it makes possible are the [rub routes](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) of
  the passing chapters), and creating it *late* means the defense can't line up in its planned
  answer to bunch until it's almost too late to communicate it.

**And the timing word: motion at the snap.**
[**Motion at the snap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion-at-the-snap) isn't a path. It
means the player is *still moving* when the ball is snapped. Jet, fly, rocket, orbit, glide and
return motion are almost always run this way; zoom and short motion usually aren't. The distinction
matters so much in the modern game that it gets its own section later in the chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In *Madden*, you can send almost any player in motion from a menu before any play, in any
direction you like. Real NFL motion is almost never improvised. It is written into the play call
("Gun Trips Right, *Z Jet*, 26 Zone", where 26 Zone is a zone run to the right), rehearsed dozens of times in practice so that the snap
arrives when the motion man reaches an exact spot, and paired with the play it is meant to help.
The quarterback's job isn't to *choose* the motion. It's to *read what the defense does* with it,
and to snap the ball at the right instant.
:::

## Job 1: asking man or zone

Start with the question in the opening scene. When a receiver goes in motion, the defense has
three basic ways to deal with him, and each one looks different.

### Travel: somebody goes with him

In man coverage each defender has a receiver, so the simplest answer to motion is for that
defender to go with him. A defender who follows a man in motion across the formation is said to
[**travel**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-travel-man-defender-follows-motion) with him.

::: {#cell-fig-jet-vs-man .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
LAT_J, WIN_J = (-20.0, 20.0), (-8.0, 15.5)
JET = [(-1.5, 15.0), (-2.4, 10.0), (-2.9, 5.5), (-3.0, 2.6)]          # Z's motion: ends 2.6 yd short of the QB
SWEEP = [(-3.1, -1.0), (-3.0, -6.0), (-1.8, -10.5), (0.5, -14.0), (3.5, -16.4), (7.5, -17.4)]
JET_T = [-2.3, -1.1, 0.0, 2.9]            # the man strip; the zone strip uses its own times


def jet_offense(p):
    """The same offensive play in both jet diagrams: jet motion by Z, then a jet sweep to the left."""
    p.motion("Z", pts=[(d - JET[0][0], w - JET[0][1]) for d, w in JET[1:]], speed=6.5)
    p.run("Z", [(d - JET[-1][0], w - JET[-1][1]) for d, w in SWEEP], speed=8.5)
    p.pitch("Z", t=0.5)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(0.25, -0.8)])
    p.block("Y", pts=[(0.4, -0.8)])
    p.run("RB", [(0.9, 1.0), (1.8, 3.2), (2.6, 5.0)], speed=5.5, delay=0.3)  # fakes inside zone the other way
    p.block("X", pts=[(3.2, 0.6)], speed=3.5)                                # blocks the corner
    p.block("H", pts=[(2.4, 1.2)], speed=3.5)


def jet_vs_man():
    dfn = front4() + [
        D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.3, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 15.3, "CB"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.6, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 6.4, "SS"),
        D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
        D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(gun_2x1_te(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    jet_offense(p)
    p.motion("RCB", pts=[(0.0, -5.0), (0.2, -10.0), (0.2, -11.6)])            # travels with Z, at his depth
    p.path("RCB", [(-0.4, -5.0), (-1.2, -12.0), (-1.4, -17.0)], speed=7.6, delay=0.2)
    p.path("NB", [(-1.2, -0.4)], speed=2.0)
    p.path("LCB", [(-2.4, 0.8)], speed=3.0)
    p.path("WILL", [(-0.6, 1.8), (-1.0, 3.6)], speed=4.0, delay=0.35)      # man on the back: goes with his fake
    p.path("MIKE", [(-0.8, -3.5), (-1.4, -6.5)], speed=4.5, delay=0.35)
    p.path("FS", [(-3.0, -5.5), (-5.0, -10.0)], speed=6.0, delay=0.3)
    p.path("SS", [(-0.8, -1.5)], speed=3.0, delay=0.2)
    p.highlight("RCB", color=style.THIRD)
    return schedule(p, {"Z": (-2.3, 0.0), "RCB": (-2.2, 0.0)})


show_play(jet_vs_man(), JET_T,
          ["1 · Set: the corner (ringed) is over Z", "2 · Z goes in jet motion; the corner travels",
           "3 · Snap: the corner is trailing Z, deep", "4 · Z turns the edge; the corner is late"],
          phases([(-2.0, "set: the corner is over Z"), (-0.05, "jet motion: the corner travels with him"),
                  (0.25, "snap: the corner trails a receiver at full speed"), (1.6, "jet sweep: the corner chases"),
                  (9, "Z turns the edge outside the corner")]),
          lateral=LAT_J, window=WIN_J, ghosts=("RCB",), ghost_t=-2.3)
```

Jet motion against man coverage (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates). The defense is in Cover 1: each defender has a receiver, and one free safety (FS) stays deep in the middle. When Z sprints across in jet motion, his cornerback (ringed) travels with him, step for step, at his own depth: that is the man coverage giving itself away. At the snap (panel 3) the corner is still on the right of the ball, nine yards deep, trailing a receiver who is already at full speed. The ball is flipped to Z on a jet sweep; the running back fakes a run the other way, and the linebacker who has him in man coverage goes with the fake. In panel 4 Z has turned upfield outside the blocked left corner, and the travelling corner, who had to stop running sideways and redirect, is a step inside and behind him. Faint lines are paths so far; the dashed outline is where the corner started. The defensive linemen are left standing to keep the picture readable.
:::
:::


To the quarterback, a corner running across the formation is about the loudest signal a defense
can send. A zone defender has no reason to leave his area to follow one receiver across the
field, so a traveller almost always means **man coverage**.

Why travel at all, if it's so obvious? Because it keeps the defense simple. The matchups the
coaches planned all week (our best corner on their best receiver) survive any motion, and nobody
has to make a new call in the last two seconds. That's a real advantage against a team that
motions on most snaps.

The price shows in the last two panels. At the snap the traveller is *trailing* a receiver who
is already running at full speed, and he himself is moving *sideways*, so the moment Z turns
upfield the corner has to stop, redirect and chase; by panel 4 he is a step inside and behind.
Anything that goes toward the side the motion is heading (a jet sweep, a flat route, a wheel up
the sideline) is a race the defender begins already losing. And when the corner crosses the
formation he ends up somewhere he wasn't built to play, near the box, where a run might come
straight at him. That's why many man defenses don't travel on every motion: on a full-speed jet
across the formation, they **exchange** instead, passing him to a teammate on the other side
(more on that in a moment).

### Bump and spin: the zone answer

A zone defense doesn't care who the receiver is; it cares where he is. So when a receiver
crosses the formation, nobody follows him. The defenders **adjust their spacing**, each moving
over one spot toward the motion, and the safeties may rotate so that the side the motion is
heading to gets an extra man.

::: {#cell-fig-jet-vs-zone .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def jet_vs_zone():
    dfn = front4() + [
        D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 15.5, "CB"),
        D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.8, "NB"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.2, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
        D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -9.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 9.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(gun_2x1_te(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    jet_offense(p)
    p.motion("WILL", to=(4.3, -5.2))           # bump: each linebacker a step toward the motion
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, -1.2))
    p.motion("FS", to=(8.0, -11.0))            # spin: motion-side safety down ...
    p.motion("SS", to=(13.5, 0.5))             # ... the other to the deep middle
    p.motion("RCB", to=(8.0, 15.0))
    p.path("NB", [(-1.0, -0.5)], speed=2.0)
    p.path("LCB", [(-1.2, -0.3)], speed=2.0)
    p.path("FS", [(-3.5, -2.6), (-6.5, -3.4)], speed=6.5, delay=0.05)      # the force player
    p.path("WILL", [(-0.5, -2.0), (-1.0, -3.2)], speed=5.5, delay=0.15)
    p.path("MIKE", [(-0.4, -2.0), (-1.0, -3.5)], speed=4.5, delay=0.25)
    p.path("SS", [(-1.0, -4.0)], speed=4.0, delay=0.3)
    p.path("RCB", [(1.0, 0.0)], speed=3.0)
    p.highlight("FS", "SS", "WILL", "MIKE", color=style.THIRD)
    return schedule(p, {"Z": (-2.3, 0.0), "WILL": (-1.7, -0.4), "MIKE": (-1.6, -0.4), "FS": (-1.5, 0.0),
                        "SS": (-1.5, 0.0), "RCB": (-1.6, -0.3)})


show_play(jet_vs_zone(), [-2.3, -0.6, 0.0, 1.8],
          ["1 · Set: two deep safeties", "2 · Nobody follows Z; linebackers bump over",
           "3 · Snap: one safety down, one to the middle", "4 · The spun safety is waiting at the edge"],
          phases([(-2.0, "set: two deep safeties"), (-1.4, "jet motion: nobody follows Z"),
                  (-0.05, "bump and spin: linebackers slide, safeties rotate"),
                  (0.25, "snap: one high, an extra man on the motion side"), (9, "the spun safety meets the sweep")]),
          lateral=LAT_J, window=WIN_J, ghosts=("FS", "SS"), ghost_t=-2.3)
```

The same jet motion and jet sweep against a zone defense (simulated, in Big Data Bowl tracking coordinates). The defense starts two-high: one deep safety on each side. When Z goes in motion, nobody follows him. The two linebackers (W and M) bump a step or two toward the side Z is heading, and the safeties spin: the one on that side (FS) comes down toward the line, and the other (SS) rotates to the deep middle, so the shell turns into one-high. The right corner stays home over empty grass. At the snap the defense has an extra player on the side of the sweep, and the safety who spun down is waiting at the edge. Ringed players are the ones to watch; dashed outlines are where the safeties started. (This defense starts two-high and the man defense above started one-high; that difference is not the lesson. What separates them is who follows Z.)
:::
:::


Two things happened, and both have names.

- **The bump.** The linebackers each slid a step toward the motion. A
  [**bump**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bump-defensive-adjustment) is defenders shuffling
  one spot toward the motion instead of following it, each taking over a new area or a new
  receiver. Nobody crossed the formation; everyone just *re-spaced*. Coaches also call it a slide
  or a shuffle.
- **The spin.** The two safeties rotated. A
  [**spin**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion) is one safety
  coming down while the other moves to the deep middle, so two deep safeties become one. The
  safety who comes down is *usually* the one on the side the motion is heading to, as here, but
  some calls rotate the other way on purpose, and the safety who comes down may stop in the
  middle of the field rather than out wide. (The rotation itself, and every variety of it, is
  taught in
  [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).)

Why answer motion this way? Because it keeps the *numbers* right without sending anyone on a
long run. Once the motion is over there will be more receivers on the left, so the defense moves
more men to the left. Notice the timing in the strip: at the snap Z is still just right of the
ball, yet the defense has already shifted. It moves to where the jet is *heading*, not where he
is, because a defender who waits for Z to arrive is too late. The safety who spins down becomes an extra defender on the motion side, the man who
stops the jet sweep in the fourth panel. Every receiver is still inside somebody's area, and no
defender ended up on the wrong side of the formation.

The price: the defense has shown its hand. Nobody travelled, so it's probably zone. The safeties
spun, so it's probably one-high now, with three deep defenders (the two corners and the middle
safety) and four or five underneath, the shape of
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd). The side the motion *left* is thinner
than it was, with a corner standing alone over empty grass. And the spin took time: a safety who
must cover the deep middle had to run eight or nine yards before the snap, which is exactly why
offenses love to snap the ball while he is still running.

### The man/zone indicator, and the running back version

Put the two pictures together and you have the
[**man/zone indicator**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-zone-indicator): reading the
defense's reaction to motion as a clue to its coverage.

| What the defense does with the motion | What it suggests |
|---|---|
| One defender runs with the motion man (**travel**) | Man coverage |
| Defenders slide over without following (**bump**) | Usually zone, but a man defense that **exchanges** looks the same; check where the slid defenders end up (next section) |
| A safety comes down and the other goes to the middle (**spin**) | A rotation to one-high (often Cover 3, or man with one deep safety if someone also travelled) |
| Safeties don't move at all | The shell you see may be the shell you get, or the rotation is coming at the snap |

: Reading the defense's answer to motion. Each row is a hint, not a guarantee; the next section explains why. {#tbl-indicator}

The cleanest version of the test doesn't use a receiver at all. Motion the **running back out of
the backfield** to a wide spot, leaving the quarterback alone (an empty formation). In man
coverage, someone is assigned to that back, usually a linebacker, and that linebacker has to walk
out of the box with him. In zone, the defender already standing out there (a nickel back or an
outside linebacker) simply takes him, and the linebackers stay home. A linebacker walking out to
the numbers with a running back is one of the most reliable pre-snap tells in football (and when
it doesn't happen, the next section shows you what to check before you call zone). It also
tells the quarterback that the middle of the field has one fewer defender in it, which is why
quarterbacks who can run love to see it.

The same reading works when the **tight end** motions. In man, whoever has him (often a safety or
a linebacker) goes with him; in zone, nobody follows and the defense re-declares its strength
toward his new side. Because the tight end is also the run strength, expect the front to shift
with him as well as the coverage.

These are this book's words. Defensive staffs have their own: following the motion man is also
called **locking** or **tracking** him, the man-coverage hand-off a **switch**, and the safety
rotation a **rotate**; when two defenders swap two receivers who cross, the call is a
[banjo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo).[^svec] If you read a breakdown that uses
different words, match the shapes, not the labels.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The man/zone indicator exists because **coverage is the defense's best-kept secret, and motion is
the cheapest way to make it leak.** A defense can hide its coverage while everyone stands still.
It can't avoid *reacting* to a player who moves, and each way of reacting has a different shape.
For the offense the information is worth a lot: man coverage invites crossing routes, rubs and
quarterback runs; zone invites throws into the gaps between defenders. A concrete version: the
call has two receivers crossing on one side and a seam route between the linebackers; if the
motion says man, the quarterback expects the crossers to rub their defenders off and throws to
the one who comes free; if it says zone, he looks for the seam in the hole between the
linebackers. When the motion **sets early**, the quarterback has time for more: with a
[kill call](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) or a built-in
[check](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) he can swap the play for one that suits
the answer. When the motion is **at the snap**, the answer arrives too late to change the play; it
feeds only his read after the snap. Motion that sets early buys a check; motion at the snap buys
a head start.
:::

### When the indicator lies

Defensive coordinators know exactly what you just learned, and they spend their careers making
it unreliable. Three counters are worth knowing now; the full treatment is in
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).

**Man defenses that exchange.** A man defense doesn't have to travel. Many play man with a rule
that says, in effect, "if he crosses the formation, pass him on." That is an
[**exchange**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-exchange-man-coverage-on-motion): nobody follows
the motion man across; instead the defenders slide one spot over and swap receivers, so the
defender on the side he arrives at picks him up and the one he left behind takes a new job. The
coverage is still man, but nobody ran across the field, so from the stands it looks exactly like a
zone bump. Defenses often decide this by the *kind* of motion: they might travel on a short
motion (cheap to follow) and exchange on a full-speed jet (expensive to chase).

::: {#cell-fig-bump-or-exchange .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
LAT_E, WIN_E = (-18.0, 18.0), (-6.6, 15.5)
H_SET = (-1.5, 5.8)
START = {"NB": (5.0, -9.5), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "SS": (7.0, 9.5)}
AFTER = {
    "zone": {"NB": (5.5, -5.6), "MIKE": (6.2, 3.0), "SS": (7.5, 12.4)},
    "man": {"NB": (6.0, -1.5), "MIKE": (3.2, 5.0), "SS": (3.6, 8.4)},
}
EYES = {"zone": {"NB": "QB", "MIKE": "QB", "SS": "QB"}, "man": {"MIKE": "H", "SS": "Y"}}



def slide_panel(ax, kind):
    off = [q.moved(d=H_SET[0], w=H_SET[1]) if q.key == "H" else q for q in gun_2x2_spread()]
    pos = {**START, **AFTER[kind]}
    dfn = front4(sde=5.0) + [
        D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -15.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 15.5, "CB"),
        D("NB", "NB", *pos["NB"], "NB"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", *pos["MIKE"], "M"),
        D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -3.0, "W"), D("SS", "SS", *pos["SS"], "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.5, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=None)
    for k, tgt in EYES[kind].items():
        p.read(tgt, key=k)
    p.highlight("MIKE", color=style.THIRD)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT_E, window=WIN_E)
    no_numbers(ax)
    P = P_of(fld, p)
    ghost_marker(ax, *P(-1.5, -9.0), "H", fld.pts_per_yard(), side="off")
    mpath(ax, P, [(-1.5, -9.0), (-2.8, -5.0), (-3.0, 2.0), (-2.4, 4.8), (-1.6, 5.4)])
    for k in ("NB", "MIKE", "SS"):
        if np.hypot(*np.subtract(START[k], AFTER[kind][k])) > 1.0:
            ghost_marker(ax, *P(*START[k]), dict(NB="NB", MIKE="M", SS="SS")[k], fld.pts_per_yard())
            dpath(ax, P, START[k], AFTER[kind][k])
    return P


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.75))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("zone", "man")):
    P = slide_panel(ax, kind)
    if kind == "zone":
        ax.set_title("1  Zone bump (Cover 3)", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
        callout(ax, P, "sits in a space,\n5-7 yds, eyes on QB", (11.0, 8.6), (6.6, 3.6), fs=6.6, ec=style.THIRD)
    else:
        ax.set_title("2  Man exchange (Cover 1)", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
        callout(ax, P, "squared up on H,\nclose and inside", (10.6, 9.0), (3.9, 5.3), fs=6.6, ec=style.THIRD)
        callout(ax, P, "NB: now the free\ndefender, middle", (10.6, -9.0), (6.6, -2.4), fs=6.6)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

How do you tell them apart? Not by the slide itself, which is the same, but by **where the slid
defenders end up**:

- **Distance and leverage.** In man, the defender who picked up the motion man stops close to him
  (often two to four yards off) and on one side of him, usually inside, squared up to *that
  receiver*. In zone, he stops at area depth (five to seven yards) in the *space between*
  receivers, and doesn't seem to care which one is nearest.
- **Eyes.** A man defender looks at his receiver; a zone defender looks into the backfield at the
  quarterback. On a tight shot you can often see which.
- **Everyone else.** Man teams tend to show it elsewhere too: corners pressed or tight with inside
  leverage, a single deep safety. If one defender exchanged and the rest look like man, believe
  man.
- **After the snap.** The final answer: man defenders turn and run with receivers, zone defenders
  drop to spots. That is a replay check, not a pre-snap one, but it is how you keep score.

One practical limit: the standard broadcast angle, the high sideline camera behind the offense
that [How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) described,
usually shows the box and the slot defenders at the snap, but often not the far corner or the
deep safeties. A linebacker walking out, or a nickel travelling, you can read live. A spin, or a
corner on the far side, you usually confirm on the replay or the All-22.

**Zone defenses that follow.** Modern zones are [pattern-matching](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)
coverages: each defender starts with an area but plays the receiver who comes into it like man
coverage. Under some of those rules a defender follows the motion man a few steps before passing
him on. The quarterback sees a defender move with the motion and thinks *man*; the coverage is
zone.

**Fake spins.** A safety spins down with the motion, the quarterback concludes "one-high," and at
the snap the safety backs out again into a two-high shell. Defenses that disguise heavily rehearse
every rotation from several starting pictures for exactly this reason.

That last counter is why offenses have pushed motion closer and closer to the snap. If the ball
is snapped while the motion man is still running, the defense has to react *once*, at full
speed, with no time for a second move. A defender who travels at the snap really is chasing; a
safety who spins at the snap really is rotating. Motion at the snap doesn't make the defense tell
the truth, but it leaves much less time to lie.

Is the indicator wearing out, now that almost every offense motions on most plays and every
defense has drilled its answers for years? Probably somewhat, but there is no clean public
measure of it yet. [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd)
shows how to measure a defense's lie with tracking data, and
[Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)
how to check a team's motion habits against its coverage. For watching, treat the indicator as
one strong clue to combine with the shell and the alignment, never as the answer.

## Job 2: changing the strength and the numbers

The second job of motion is simpler and older: change the formation after the defense has lined
up against it.

Defenses align to the offense's **strength** (usually the tight end's side, or the side with more
receivers), and they assign their pass defenders by counting receivers on each side. When a player
crosses the formation, both of those change, and somebody on the defense has to move.

This is the arithmetic every motion forces. **The defense has eleven players, and each one it
moves toward the motion comes from somewhere.** If a linebacker walks out, the box gets lighter,
and the run game gets the numbers advantage that
[A First Look at Defense](02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) taught you to count. If a
safety rotates over, the deep coverage changes and the lone receiver on the other side may be in
a one-on-one with no help over the top. If the corner follows, the coverage is man and the
quarterback knows it. Offensive coordinators design motions to make the defense choose among
those three, then call plays that attack whichever spot the defense gave up.

The **trade** does the same thing to the defensive *front*. Defensive linemen and linebackers set
their alignment to the tight end: the bigger end lines up across from him, the strong-side
linebacker walks out to his side, and the strong safety cheats toward him. When the tight end
trades sides, all of that has to flip in the two or three seconds before the snap, which is why
offenses that like to run at the strength love to trade at the last moment. A defense that
flips late and loses a gap in the confusion is a run waiting to happen; a defense that refuses to
flip has its strength on the wrong side. The defense does get one guaranteed beat: a trade is a
shift, so the offense must then stand still for a full second. Defenses use it by **declaring
the strength late**, not setting the front until the shift is over, and offenses answer by
following the trade with a motion, the "shift, freeze, motion" sequence from
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd).

The **shift to bunch** attacks the coverage the same way. Most defenses have a pre-planned answer
to a bunch, because man coverage against three receivers in a tight triangle invites collisions
and picks. If the bunch appears with two seconds left, that answer has to be called, heard and
applied by four or five defenders at once.

Motion changes the numbers for the **run game** too. A receiver or a fullback who motions toward
the ball can become an extra blocker: a lead blocker through the hole, or a receiver arriving
with momentum to [crack](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) back on the
defender who has to set the edge. Either way the offense has added a blocker, or a better
blocking angle, on the side of the run, and every player who arrives in the box adds a gap the
defense must fill. The blocks themselves are taught in
[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) and
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

### Why shift instead of motion?

The trade and the bunch are shifts, not motions, and a shift buys different things. **Several
players can move at once**: the tight end, a back and a receiver can all change spots, so the
offense can build a formation no single motion could reach (the strength flipped, the back on the
other side, a receiver now on the line), and the defense has to re-declare almost everything. It
also lets the offense line up in one look, watch the defense align to it, and then move into the
formation it really wants. The price is the **one-second freeze**: after a shift everyone must be
set for a full second, so the shift itself gives nobody a running start, and the defense gets a
full beat to re-set. That is why
the modern pattern is so often both: shift to change the formation, freeze, then motion one man
to get the running start and ask the man-or-zone question.

## Jobs 3 and 4: the running start and leverage

The third and fourth jobs are about the moment the ball is snapped, and they are really one idea:
**a player who is moving at the snap begins the play somewhere the defense didn't plan for, at a
speed the defense doesn't have.**

### The running start

How big is a running start? You can estimate it with simple physics. A football player
accelerates roughly like a sprinter: hard at first, then levelling off near his top speed. The
chart below compares two receivers with the same top speed, one starting from a standstill and
one already running at jet-motion pace when the ball is snapped.

::: {#cell-fig-head-start .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
TAU, VMAX = 0.55, 10.0
t = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 201)


def dist(v0):
    """Distance covered by t, starting at speed v0 and approaching VMAX exponentially."""
    return VMAX * t - (VMAX - v0) * TAU * (1 - np.exp(-t / TAU))


still, moving = dist(0.0), dist(7.0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.8))
ax.plot(t, moving, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.2, label="Already moving at the snap (7 yd/s)")
ax.plot(t, still, color=style.MUTED, lw=2.2, label="Standing still at the snap")
for tt in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5):
    i = int(tt * 100)
    ax.plot([tt, tt], [still[i], moving[i]], color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9)
    ax.text(tt + 0.03, (still[i] + moving[i]) / 2, f"+{moving[i] - still[i]:.1f} yd", fontsize=7.4,
            color=style.INK, va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("Seconds after the snap", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Yards covered", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2.0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 20.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

Three yards in a second is enormous. It is the difference between a jet sweep that reaches the
edge before the defensive end can widen and one that is tackled for no gain; between a receiver
who is covered and one who is open. A defender can match a receiver's speed. He can't match a
head start, because he isn't allowed to have one: he must react to the snap like everybody else.

One catch: the head start points **in the direction of the motion**, which the rules make
sideways or backward. A play that keeps going that way gets nearly all of it: a jet sweep, a flat
route, a wheel up the sideline, a crack block. A receiver who has to turn upfield, or cut back the
other way, spends some of it on the turn, and a return motion deliberately throws it away to
punish the defender who matched it. That is why offenses kept looking for motions that end
pointed nearly upfield at the snap, which is exactly what the "cheat motion" later in this chapter
was about.

In the model, the lead depends on two things: how fast the motion is run, and how long the
standing player still needs to reach top speed. That is why offenses with very fast receivers
motion so much: a head start is worth most to receivers who run their motion at a high speed and
still have a long acceleration phase ahead of them, and very fast receivers tend to do both. It's
also why defenses hate pressing a
receiver who is in motion: [press coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) (a defender lined up right on the receiver to jam
him at the line)
depends on getting hands on a man who is standing still. You can't jam somebody who is already
running past you.

### Leverage: start where he didn't plan for

Every defender aligns with [leverage](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd), a deliberate position inside or outside his receiver
that tells him which way to force him and where his help is. That alignment is planned against a
receiver who is standing still. Motion changes it in a way the defender can't fully fix:

- A defender who **travels** with motion is, by definition, *behind* the receiver in the
  direction he is moving. A receiver moving inside at the snap (glide motion) is already inside
  his defender, which helps routes that break inside. A receiver moving outside at the snap
  (orbit, rocket) is already outside his.
- A defender who **bumps** is standing in a spot chosen for the *old* formation, a step or two
  from where he would have lined up if the offense had started in the new one.

The most famous way to exploit the first of these is the return motion.

::: {#cell-fig-return-motion .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def return_vs_man():
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R"),
                    O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -7.5, "H"),
                    O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
    dfn = front4() + [
        D("LCB", "CB", 1.5, -13.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 2.5, 12.5, "CB"),
        D("NB", "NB", 2.5, -7.6, "NB"), D("SS", "SS", 3.6, 4.2, "SS"),
        D("FS", "FS", 5.6, -1.4, "FS"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 3.3, 1.7, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 3.3, -2.6, "W")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=105, to_go=5)
    p.motion("Z", pts=[(-0.1, -2.8), (-0.2, -5.0)])                       # in toward the ball
    p.motion("RCB", pts=[(-0.1, -2.7), (-0.2, -4.8)])                     # travels with him
    p.route("Z", r.path((-0.2, 2.6), (0.8, 6.6), (3.2, 8.8), (6.8, 9.6)), side=1, speed=7.5)  # back out
    p.path("RCB", [(-0.1, -1.1), (-0.2, 1.8), (0.4, 5.5), (1.4, 8.0)], speed=5.6, delay=0.2)
    p.dropback(1.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=0.55)
    p.route("X", r.fade(9)); p.route("H", r.path((2.5, 0.5), (5.0, 3.0)))
    p.route("Y", r.path((2.5, -0.3), (4.0, -0.5)))
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, 1.0)])
    for k, dw in (("LT", -0.5), ("LG", -0.2), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 0.2), ("RT", 0.5)):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, dw)])
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE", "MIKE", "WILL"):
        p.rush(k, speed=2.6)
    p.path("LCB", [(1.5, -0.6), (5.0, -1.6)], speed=6.5)
    p.path("NB", [(1.0, -1.5), (2.5, -3.0)], speed=5.5)
    p.path("SS", [(1.0, -0.3), (2.0, -0.8)], speed=4.5)                    # man on Y
    p.path("FS", [(-1.0, -0.5)], speed=2.0)                               # has the back; the back blocks, so he sits
    p.highlight("RCB", color=style.THIRD)
    return schedule(p, {"Z": (-1.4, 0.0), "RCB": (-1.35, 0.0)})

          ["1 · Goal to go: Z starts in toward the ball", "2 · Snap: the corner (ringed) followed; Z plants",
```

Look at the defender's problem in the third panel. A man defender's whole technique is to mirror
the receiver, and here the receiver has reversed direction at the one instant the defender can't
anticipate. Every step the corner took following the motion is now a step in the wrong direction.
Against zone the same motion does little (the zone defenders bump and then sit in their areas),
which is why return motion is called most often when the offense expects man coverage: near the
goal line, on third-and-short, against blitzes.

### The jet as a fake

Most jet motions end with the ball going to somebody else. That's not wasted motion. A receiver
sprinting across the formation at the snap is a threat to run a sweep, so the defenders responsible
for the edge on that side must take a step toward him, and the linebackers' eyes go with him. A
run the other way, or a play-action pass behind the flowing linebackers, now has one fewer
defender in its way, or one who is a step late. Offenses that run a lot of jet motion build their
plays in pairs: the jet sweep itself, and the plays that take advantage of the defense
*respecting* the jet sweep. That pairing, and why the sweep has to be run often enough to stay
believable, is the subject of [Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

## Job 5: stressing the defense's communication

The fifth job doesn't show up on a diagram, but defensive coaches talk about it constantly. Every
change in the formation obliges the defense to **re-communicate**: the linebacker who makes the
front call (usually the Mike, who tells the linemen which way to align) re-declares the strength;
the safeties re-call the coverage check (the pre-planned adjustment of the called coverage to the
formation in front of them, since many coverages change when a 2x2 becomes a 3x1); the corners
confirm who has whom; and in a man defense the players involved have to agree in one word whether
they're travelling or exchanging.

All of that happens with the offense deciding when the ball moves. If the motion starts with ten
seconds on the play clock, the defense has time. If it starts with three, and the ball is
snapped as the motion man passes the quarterback, the defense has one chance to get every call
right, often in a loud stadium. The typical failure isn't dramatic: two defenders take the same
receiver and nobody takes another, or a safety rotates the wrong way. But one blown assignment is
usually all an NFL offense needs for a big play.

The stress runs both ways. The offense, too, has to execute the motion perfectly: the motion man
has to start on the right signal, run at the right pace and be at the right spot when the ball is
snapped, and the center has to snap it at precisely that moment. You can often see the machinery
on the broadcast. In the shotgun, the quarterback commonly starts the motion with a **leg lift**
or a tap of his heel or hand, with no words at all, and the snap then comes on a count the center
and quarterback have timed to the motion man's landmark.[^leglift] A motion that arrives early
leaves the receiver standing and waiting; one that arrives late leaves the quarterback holding
the snap while the defense sorts itself out. And a rhythm that never varies is one the defense
can learn, which matters in the next section.

## Motion at the snap

Everything above points to one conclusion: **the later the motion, the more it's worth.** A
motion that ends two seconds before the snap gives the defense two seconds to adjust, disguise
and re-communicate. A motion that is still going when the ball is snapped gives it none. Through
the late 2010s and 2020s, NFL offenses learned that lesson fast.

ESPN Analytics, which charts specifically whether a player is moving at the snap, found that the
average team did it on about **4%** of its plays in 2017 and about **22%** in 2023.[^espnsnap]
The 2023 Miami Dolphins, coordinated by head coach Mike McDaniel, were the extreme: early that
season ESPN had them with a player in motion at the snap on **59%** of plays, by far the most of
any team since ESPN began tracking in 2017.[^miami59] By 2025 other offenses had caught up:
according to Next Gen Stats, the Atlanta Falcons under offensive coordinator Zac Robinson led the
league in 2025 with motion at the snap on **60.8%** of their plays (and used some pre-snap motion
on **70.1%**, sixth in the league).[^atl]

Why is motion at the snap so valuable? Because it does jobs 3, 4 and 5 at full strength at once:
the running start is at full value, the leverage can't be fixed after the snap, and the
defense's adjustment, with its communication, has to happen in real time, with no time left to
disguise.

And what does it cost? The motion man can't be a pass blocker, and his route has to start from
wherever the motion takes him. The timing has to be perfect on every snap. The quarterback gives
up the chance to **check the play** after seeing the defense's reaction: the information arrives in
time for his read after the snap, not for his call before it. And it hands the
defense one piece of information that defensive coordinators have learned to use: **if the snap
comes when the motion man reaches the quarterback, the defense knows when the snap is coming.**
A defense that times its own movement (a blitzer creeping up, a safety rotating) to the motion
man's arrival can move at the last instant without risking an offside penalty. Writing in
January 2024, Ben Solak of The Ringer pointed out that the two defenses then meeting in the AFC
Championship Game, Steve Spagnuolo's Chiefs and Mike Macdonald's Ravens, ranked first (Baltimore)
and sixth (Kansas City) in EPA per play allowed on snaps with motion, according to Next Gen
Stats, and that both made a habit of changing the whole picture as the motion triggered the
snap.[^ringer] The arms race moves to the last half-second.

### The "cheat motion" and the 2024 rule language

Motion at the snap reached the edge of the rulebook in 2023. Instead of sending a fast receiver
all the way across the formation, the Dolphins (and soon the 49ers and Rams) lined him up tight,
close to the tackle, and had him take a short, quick motion *outward*, toward his own sideline,
just before the snap, so that he could turn upfield at full speed the instant the ball moved: a
sprinter's rolling start. Kyle Shanahan called it a "little cheat motion" and admitted the 49ers
had copied it "in Week 2 after we saw it."[^cheat] Reporters noticed that Tyreek Hill sometimes
seemed to be turning upfield a fraction early, but he was never flagged for illegal motion all
season.

Was it legal? The rule said a player may not be moving *toward* the line at the snap, and the
officials judged that these motions were sideways at the moment the ball moved. For 2024 the
league added language to the false-start rule that was widely reported as aimed at the trick. An
eligible receiver who is **on the line** and moves backward or changes his stance (from a
two-point to a three-point stance, or back) now has to come to a **complete stop** before the
snap, or it's a false start; a player in the backfield who changes his stance doesn't have to
stop, as long as his movement isn't abrupt (a false start) or forward (illegal
motion).[^cheat2024]

Read that language next to the trick and you'll notice they don't quite meet. The cheat motion was
run by a receiver who had to be *off* the line to go in motion at all, moving sideways; the new sentence is about receivers *on* the
line stepping back or changing stance. League officials later told reporters exactly that: it was
a clarification, not a rule change, aimed at abrupt stance changes, and it did not outlaw
sideways motion that turns upfield at the snap. So the honest summary is that the cheat motion
itself survived. What the clarification ruled out was a neighbouring way to steal a start: a
receiver on the line rocking back or dropping into a stance at the last instant.

## The rulebook: NFL, college and Canada

You have the NFL's rule from the "You'll need" box: one backfield player, moving parallel to or
away from the line. Two details are worth adding.

First, a player who is *on the line* can't go in motion at all without first getting off it, and
that has real consequences. In Super Bowl LVII, when the Chiefs wanted to run their return-motion
play a second time, Patrick Mahomes signalled for Kadarius Toney to go in motion, but Toney was
lined up on the line of scrimmage and couldn't. Toney pointed across the field at Skyy Moore, who
was in the backfield, and Moore went instead; he scored the touchdown.[^wrongformation]

Second, the rule's purpose is the same as the one-second set's: **the offense may move before the
snap, but it may not get a running start at the line of scrimmage.** A sideways head start is
allowed; a forward one isn't.

| | NFL | NCAA (college) | CFL (Canada) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Players in motion at the snap | One | One | Any number of backfield players |
| Direction | Parallel to or away from the line | Not toward the opponent's goal line | Any direction, **including toward the line** |
| Who may move | A backfield player | A backfield player | Backfield players (not the quarterback) |

: Motion rules in three codes. American college rules match the NFL's in substance; Canadian rules are different in kind. {#tbl-motion-rules}

College football's rule is essentially the same as the NFL's: one player, not moving toward the
opponent's goal line at the snap, and a player who starts on the line has to become a back and come
to a complete stop before he can go in motion.[^ncaa]
The big outlier is Canadian football. In the CFL, every backfield player except the quarterback
may be in motion at the snap, in any direction, including **forward**.[^cfl] Canadian receivers
routinely hit the line of scrimmage at full speed as the ball is snapped (a "waggle"), which is
one reason the Canadian game, on a bigger field with twelve players a side, is so pass-heavy. If
you've wondered what would happen if the NFL allowed forward motion, the CFL is the experiment:
receivers that are nearly impossible to jam, and defenders who line up far off the ball to avoid
being run past.

## The motion boom, by the numbers

Motion is as old as the T formation (the Bears' man in motion in the 1940 championship game is
in [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and some coaches made
pre-snap movement a signature long before it was fashionable. Tom Landry's Cowboys of the 1960s
to 1980s famously had their offensive linemen stand up in unison and then drop back into their
stances while the backs shifted behind them, the "Landry shift," partly to hide the new backfield
alignment behind a wall of standing linemen.[^landry] But for most of NFL history motion was a
tool for particular plays, not a habit.

That changed in the late 2010s. Kyle Shanahan (49ers head coach from 2017) and Sean McVay (Rams
head coach from 2017) built offenses in which motion was part of almost every call, and as their
assistants became coordinators and head coaches around the league, the habit spread. By ESPN's
count, the 49ers used pre-snap motion on 69.1% of their plays from 2017 through 2021, the most in
the league, and on 76.9% in 2021 alone, while the league as a whole rose from 34.9% (2017) to
46.8% (2021).[^espnboom] PFF's longer shift-or-motion series, which
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) quoted, shows the same climb
to a record **63.9%** in 2025, when every team except the Giants moved someone before at least
half of its snaps.[^pff]

Why the boom? Three reasons, each from earlier in this chapter. **Defenses started hiding their
coverage better**: Next Gen Stats measured two-high (split-safety) coverage on 32.9% of plays in 2018 and
42.0% in 2025, the highest since its tracking began,[^twohigh] and two-high shells are built to rotate,
so offenses needed a way to make them commit. **The head start became more valuable** as offenses
filled with very fast receivers. And **it worked visibly** for the offenses that did it most, so
it was copied.

Here is how the 32 teams moved, in FTN's charting.

### Why the motion numbers disagree

You will see wildly different "motion rates" quoted for the same season: 22%, 55%, 64%. They are
not contradictions. They are different measurements.
