Four things make the numbers differ, and each is worth knowing before you quote one:

1. **What counts as movement.** PFF counts shifts *and* motion. FTN's `is_motion` flag means
   "motion occurred on the play before or at the time of the snap." ESPN's headline series counts
   only a player *still moving* at the snap, a much smaller set. Next Gen Stats publishes yet
   another pair, total pre-snap motion and motion at the snap: Atlanta's 70.1% and 60.8% in
   2025, quoted above.
2. **Who or what does the charting.** PFF and FTN use human charters watching video; Next Gen
   Stats uses the player-tracking chips. A human charter and a tracking threshold can disagree
   about whether a receiver's two-step shuffle "counts."
3. **Which plays are in the denominator.** All snaps, or only runs and passes? Are kneel-downs,
   spikes and penalty-only plays included? Playoffs? These shift a rate by a point or two.
4. **Which seasons exist.** FTN's charting in nflverse starts in 2022, ESPN's motion-at-the-snap
   series in 2017, PFF's runs back further.

The rule this book follows: **every motion number carries its source, and two sources never
share an axis.** When you compare teams or seasons, compare them inside one series.

### Does motion work?

The honest answer is "yes, but not in the way a simple average suggests." In FTN's data, plays
with motion and plays without it look surprisingly alike. On first and second downs in 2025,
passes with motion averaged about +0.10
[EPA](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) per play against +0.06
without, and runs about −0.05 against −0.08; in 2024 the two were nearly identical, and in 2022
passes *without* motion did better.[^epa] Teams that motion more did have slightly better
offenses in each of the four seasons, but the relationship is loose.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Motion plays gain more, so offenses should motion on every play." The averages above don't show
that, and even if they did, the comparison wouldn't prove it. Offenses *choose* when to motion:
some save it for their best-designed plays, some motion on almost everything, and defenses adjust
to teams that motion a lot. The plays with and without motion aren't a controlled experiment.
Other comparisons find more: ESPN's numbers for 2017–2023, as reported by The Ringer in 2024, had
runs with motion *at the snap* gaining about 0.11 EPA per play more than runs with no motion, and
dropbacks about 0.08 more.[^ringer2] That is a simple with-and-without comparison too, though, so
it carries the same caution.
Part of motion's value is also invisible in its own plays: a motion that always meant "run" would
be a [tell](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd), so offenses use the same
motions on different plays to keep the defense from reading them. Measuring that kind of value is
part of [Tendencies: PROE, Personnel, Motion, and Coverage](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd).
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Miami Dolphins 2023, motion at the snap"}
No offense in the tracking era moved like Mike McDaniel's 2023 Dolphins. In FTN's charting they
used motion on 79.4% of their runs and passes, the highest team-season from 2022 to 2025; ESPN had
them with a player in motion at the snap on 59% of plays early that season, a record. They
scored 70 points against Denver in Week 3, and Tyreek Hill led the NFL with 1,799 receiving
yards.[^hill]

What to notice when you watch the film: the motion is short and *timed*. Hill or Jaylen Waddle
moves a few yards, sometimes in toward the formation, sometimes out toward the sideline (the
"cheat" version), and the ball is snapped as he gets going. The defense rarely gets a clean look
at its own assignment, and Hill starts every route already running. Then watch the defenses that
slowed Miami down. The Chiefs, who beat the Dolphins twice that season (in Frankfurt in November
and in the wild-card round), mostly refused to chase: in the November game they played zone on a
season-high 61% of Miami's dropbacks, by ESPN's count, with Steve Spagnuolo's instruction to keep "22 eyeballs" on Hill, and L'Jarius Sneed matched Hill when they
did play man.[^kcmia] McDaniel was let go by Miami in January 2026 and is the Chargers'
offensive coordinator for the 2026 season.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023)"}
Two of the most famous motion plays of the decade came less than three minutes of game clock apart. In the fourth quarter
against the Eagles, Kansas City ran a play its coaches call "Corn Dog": a receiver motions in
toward the formation, then turns and runs back toward the sideline at the snap, a return motion
built to beat man coverage. Kadarius Toney caught a 5-yard touchdown on it with 12:04 left to give
the Chiefs the lead, and Skyy Moore scored from 4 yards on a mirrored version at 9:22. Both times
the Eagles were in man coverage, the defender went with the first move, and the receiver was alone
when he turned around. Kansas City won 38–35. A year later in Super Bowl LVIII the Chiefs ran a
renamed relative of the play for Mecole Hardman's winning touchdown in overtime.[^corndog]

What to notice: the motion does *two* jobs on one play. First it asks the question (did the
defender follow?), and then it attacks the answer (the defender who followed is moving the wrong
way). Andy Reid's offense has used motion that way for years, including orbit motion that loops a
receiver behind the quarterback and out to the flat, pulling defenders with him while the real
target comes open elsewhere.[^orbitkc]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2021, Deebo Samuel"}
In 2021 the 49ers motioned on 76.9% of their plays, the most in the league by ESPN's count.
Much of it went through Deebo Samuel, a wide receiver who spent part of the season lining up and
motioning into the backfield. Motion let Shanahan move Samuel from receiver to ball carrier and
back again before the snap, so the defense never knew which position it was defending. He caught
passes for 1,405 yards and ran for 365 more, with eight rushing touchdowns.[^deebo]

What to notice: the motion *creates the matchup*. When Samuel motioned from a receiver spot into the
backfield, the defender assigned to him in man coverage had to follow him into the box, where a
cornerback or safety is suddenly playing run defense against a 215-pound receiver with a head start.
Against zone, the defense now faced a backfield with two ball carriers in it, one of them very fast,
and had to respect both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2017–2025, the same look, different plays"}
McVay's Rams were not the league's most frequent motion team in his first seasons (ESPN had them
eighth from 2017 to 2021), but they made the jet motion famous, and by 2024 FTN charted
them with motion on 76.7% of their plays, the highest in the league that season. The Rams' trademark
is pairing: over a game, the same jet look comes before an outside-zone run, a jet sweep and a
play-action pass, so the motion tells the defense nothing about the play. What to notice: the
play was called in the huddle, so the defense's reaction doesn't change *this* play; it tells you
which one should work. Watch the linebackers when the jet man crosses the quarterback. If they
jump toward him, the run the other way should hit; if they stay home, expect the Rams to give it
to the jet man on a later snap.
:::

## The checklist so far

Part 2 ends here, and with it the first version of the card you will carry through the rest of
the book. Each line is a question you can answer before the snap, in the order the answers
become visible on a broadcast (the order [Personnel](02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd) introduced):
the situation first, then who is on the field, then where they line up, then what the motion
draws out of the defense, then the box and the safeties.

Two habits make the card work. **Say each answer out loud, or write it down, before the snap.**
A guess you didn't commit to can't teach you anything. And **read the lines in order.** The motion
line comes after the formation line because you can't interpret a defender's reaction until you
know what the motion did to the formation; the shell line comes last because the motion may have
changed it.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: follow the motion"}
For one quarter, every time an offensive player moves before the snap, do four things.

- **Name it.** Jet, orbit, return, zoom, glide, short, a trade, a shift? If you aren't sure, describe
  the path ("across, in front of the quarterback").
- **Watch who follows.** Pick up the defender who was across from the motion man *before* he moved.
  Did that defender travel across (T), did the defenders bump over (B), did a safety spin (S)? Write
  the letters. If it was a bump, look at where the slid defender stopped: tight on one man (an
  exchange, so man) or in a space between receivers (zone)?
- **Call it.** Man or zone? One-high or two-high at the snap? Write your call before the ball is
  snapped.
- **Note the timing.** Was the ball snapped while he was still moving (motion at the snap), or did he
  set first?

Then check your calls on the replay, or better, on the All-22 film, which shows the whole secondary.
Add a column for it in your prediction log from
[How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd). After a few games
you'll notice two things: travellers are rarer than you expect (many man defenses
[exchange](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-exchange-man-coverage-on-motion) instead), and your
calls get better when the motion is at the snap.
:::

**Man or zone? How many deep safeties? And what does the offense like about the picture?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Man coverage, with one deep safety: Cover 1, almost certainly.** Two things happened at once.
The nickel back travelled with H all the way across the formation, which a zone defender has no
reason to do: that says man. And the safeties spun: the two-high picture turned into one safety in
the deep middle and one at 8 yards in the middle of the field, a classic spot for a "robber" who
lurks underneath looking for crossing routes (see
[Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). Notice that this spin didn't drop the
safety out toward the motion side; it dropped him into the middle. Spins vary in where the down
safety lands; the part that matters for your call is that two deep became one. Travel plus spin is
the signature of man coverage disguised as two-high before the motion.

What the offense likes: H's defender is now **behind and inside** a receiver who is moving toward
the sideline at full speed. A flat route, a wheel up the sideline, or a quick throw to H the instant
the ball is snapped all start as races the nickel back is losing. On the other side, X is alone
with his corner, and with the single deep safety in the middle there is no help over the top on the
outside. Man coverage also means most defenders have their backs turned to the quarterback, so a
quarterback who can run has open grass if the routes clear out the middle.

The caution: a robber in the middle is there precisely to jump the crossing routes that beat man
coverage, so throwing a shallow cross into him is the mistake the defense is hoping for.
:::
:::

**What should the offense call here, and why does it work only because of the first half?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Give the ball to Z: the jet sweep itself.** The defense has learned that the jet is a fake and
the run is coming the other way, so it has stopped spending players on the jet. The linebackers
stay home to play the running back, and the end on Z's side has pinched inside to close the
back's path, a pre-snap tell that he means to crash. Now count the jet side. H blocks the nickel,
who is the defender responsible for turning the play back inside (the force player); X stalks the
corner; and the only unblocked defender left on that side is the safety 13 yards deep, too far
away to get to the edge before Z does. Z already has a head start; with the end inside and nobody
flowing with him, he gets the corner.

That is the logic of jet motion as a *constraint*: the fake is only worth something if the real
thing is a threat. Run the inside handoff enough and the defense ignores the jet; run the jet when
it does. Offenses build their game plans around exactly this pairing (more in
[Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd) and
[Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd)).
The defense's counter is to keep at least one player honest on the jet side: a safety who spins
toward the motion, as in the zone animation earlier, would have been waiting.
:::
:::

**The running-back test said that in man coverage a linebacker walks out with the back. Nobody
did. Is this zone? Look at where the two defenders who slid ended up.**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Probably still man coverage, Cover 1, played with an exchange.** Nobody travelled, so the
first-glance read is zone, and that is exactly what the defense wants you to think. But look at
where the slid defenders stopped. The strong safety is three yards in front of the back and just
inside him, squared up on one man. The Mike is four yards in front of Y and just inside him, also
squared up on one man. Zone defenders on that side would have stopped at area depth, five to
seven yards, *between* Y and the back, waiting for whoever came into their space. Two defenders
each pairing up with one receiver is man coverage; the defense simply passed the back to the
safety and pushed the Mike out onto Y instead of sending the Mike across with the back.

So the running-back test needs one refinement: the tell isn't "the Mike walks out", it's "**a
box defender** leaves to take a receiver". Here one did, just not the one you were watching. The
box is down to five defenders (four linemen and the Will) against five blockers, with one deep
safety behind them.

What the offense likes: a linebacker in man coverage on Y in open space, and a safety on a
running back, are both matchups the offense created on purpose; a quick option route by Y or an
out by the back is often the first read. With every defender's back turned and the middle
thinned, a quarterback scramble is open on third-and-6. The caution: an empty backfield leaves no
back to pick up an extra rusher, so if the Will or the nickel blitzes, the ball has to come out
quickly (see [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). And if at the
snap the safety and the Mike *drop* instead of turning to run with their men, the read was wrong:
log it, and look for what you missed.
:::

## Takeaways

- **Motion is never decoration.** Every motion does at least one of five jobs: it asks *man or
  zone?*, changes the strength and the numbers (receivers or blockers), gives a running start,
  creates leverage, or stresses the defense's communication. A shift moves several players and
  rebuilds the formation, but it costs a one-second freeze and gives nobody a running start.
- **Learn the shapes, not just the names.** Jet, fly and orbit cross the formation (in front of,
  behind, and looping behind the quarterback); rocket sprints a back to the edge; return goes and
  comes back; zoom crosses and sets; glide comes in and is still moving at the snap, short motion
  comes in and sets; a trade or a shift to bunch rebuilds the formation. Names vary by playbook.
- **Read the answer, then check it.** A defender who **travels** suggests man; defenders who
  **bump** suggest zone; safeties who **spin** turn two-high into one-high. But a man defense can
  **exchange**, sliding over just like a zone, so look at where the slid defenders stop: tight on
  one receiver means man, sitting in a space between receivers means zone. Pattern-matching zones
  can follow, and safeties can spin back. This read is line 4 of the checklist so far: situation →
  personnel → formation and strength → the motion response → box → shell, then log it.
- **The later the motion, the more it's worth.** Motion at the snap gives a running start worth
  about three yards in the first second (in the direction of the motion) and leaves the defense no
  time to disguise, but it also leaves the quarterback no time to check the play. NFL use of it
  rose from about 4% of plays in 2017 to over 20% by 2023 (ESPN).
- **The rules shape the motion.** American rules allow one backfield player moving sideways or
  back at the snap; Canadian rules let backs move forward. The 2024 NFL language on receivers who
  change stance on the line was a clarification that left the sideways "cheat motion" legal.
- **Motion numbers depend on the source.** PFF (any shift or motion: 63.9% in 2025), FTN (motion
  before or at the snap: 55.1%), ESPN and Next Gen Stats (motion at the snap) all measure different
  things. Quote one source at a time.
